To-the-Nile-by-Keats.title: To the Nile
To-the-Nile-by-Keats.by: by John Keats · O/L Literature Interactive Quiz

data.q: How does the speaker address the Nile at the beginning?
opts: As the father of African rivers
data.why: The opening apostrophe honours the Nile as the father of African rivers.

data.q: What does “Nurse of swart nations” suggest?
opts: The river flows only at night
data.why: “Nurse” personifies the Nile as a life-giving protector.

data.q: Which contrast shapes the sonnet?
opts: Mythic greatness and an ordinary natural river
data.why: Keats balances the Nile’s legendary image against its physical reality.

data.q: What poetic form is used?
data.why: The poem is a fourteen-line sonnet.

data.q: What does the green rush suggest?
data.why: Green vegetation reinforces the river’s fertility.

data.q: What is a central idea of the poem?
opts: Imagination changes how people see nature
data.why: The poem examines how imagination and inherited ideas shape perception.

A-Bird-came-down-the-Walk.title: A Bird Came Down the Walk
A-Bird-came-down-the-Walk.by: by Emily Dickinson · O/L Literature Interactive Quiz

data.q: What does the bird do first?
data.why: The poem opens with the bird eating an angleworm.

data.q: Why does the bird look around rapidly?
opts: It wants to attack the speaker
data.why: Its quick glances show alertness to possible danger.

data.q: What does the speaker offer the bird?
data.why: The speaker cautiously offers a crumb.

data.q: The bird’s eyes are compared to what?
data.why: The simile “frightened Beads” captures the bird’s nervous watchfulness.

data.q: How is the bird’s flight presented?
data.why: The swimming and rowing images make the flight seem smooth and effortless.

data.q: What contrast is central to the poem?
opts: The bird’s beauty and the harshness of nature
data.why: The delicate bird is also a predator living in a threatening natural world.

Farewell-to-Barn-Stack-and-Tree.title: Farewell to Barn and Stack and Tree
Farewell-to-Barn-Stack-and-Tree.by: by A. E. Housman · O/L Literature Interactive Quiz

data.q: Why must the speaker leave home?
opts: He has killed his brother Maurice
data.why: The speaker admits that Maurice lies dead with his knife in his side.

data.q: To whom does the speaker say farewell?
data.why: He directly addresses Terence throughout the farewell.

data.q: What will the mother discover?
data.why: She began the day with two sons but will be alone by night.

data.q: Which form best describes the poem?
data.why: Its narrative, quatrains, simple language and tragedy are ballad features.

data.q: What does the repeated word “bloody” emphasize?
data.why: The blood on his hand links the speaker permanently with the murder.

data.q: What creates much of the poem’s pathos?
opts: Ordinary farm life continuing after a family tragedy
data.why: Familiar rural details deepen the sadness of the sudden loss.

To-the-Evening-Star.title: To the Evening Star
To-the-Evening-Star.by: by William Blake · O/L Literature Interactive Quiz

data.q: Who is directly addressed?
data.why: The poem is an apostrophe to the evening star.

data.q: What is the star asked to wear?
data.why: The speaker imagines the star with a radiant crown.

data.q: What is the star asked to protect?
opts: The speaker’s natural surroundings at night
data.why: The speaker asks its light and dew to guard the peaceful landscape.

data.q: Which mood dominates the first part?
data.why: Gentle imperatives and luminous images create a devotional calm.

data.q: What threatens when the star withdraws?
data.why: The wolf and lion represent dangers released by darkness.

data.q: Which technique gives the star human power?
data.why: The star is treated as a guardian able to act and protect.

The-Eagle-by-Tennyson.title: The Eagle
The-Eagle-by-Tennyson.by: by Alfred, Lord Tennyson · O/L Literature Interactive Quiz

data.q: Where does the eagle stand?
opts: Close to the sun on a crag
data.why: The eagle grips a high rock in a remote landscape.

data.q: What does “crooked hands” describe?
data.why: The metaphor makes the eagle’s talons resemble powerful hands.

data.q: How does the sea appear from above?
data.why: Distance makes the moving sea look wrinkled.

data.q: What surrounds the eagle?
data.why: The repeated blue imagery emphasizes height and isolation.

data.q: How does the eagle descend?
data.why: The final simile conveys sudden speed and tremendous power.

data.q: What qualities are most strongly presented?
data.why: The compact images make the eagle solitary, controlled and majestic.

War-is-Kind.title: War Is Kind
War-is-Kind.by: by Stephen Crane · O/L Literature Interactive Quiz

data.q: Why is the title ironic?
opts: The poem shows war’s cruelty, not kindness
data.why: The repeated claim conflicts sharply with the suffering described.

data.q: Whom does the speaker address?
opts: People grieving for loved ones killed in war
data.why: The speaker addresses a maiden, a child and a mother.

data.q: What does the repeated refrain achieve?
opts: It makes the deaths seem unimportant
data.why: Repetition makes “war is kind” increasingly bitter and unbelievable.

data.q: How are soldiers trained to think?
opts: Killing and dying are glorious duties
data.why: The battle creed conditions soldiers to accept violence and death.

data.q: What do vivid death images oppose?
data.why: Physical suffering undercuts abstract words about glory and virtue.

data.q: What is the poem’s main attitude to war?
data.why: Irony and brutal imagery condemn war and its propaganda.

I-know-why-the-Caged-Bird-Sings.title: I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings
I-know-why-the-Caged-Bird-Sings.by: by Maya Angelou · O/L Literature Interactive Quiz

data.q: What does the free bird symbolize?
data.why: Its unrestricted movement represents liberty and opportunity.

data.q: What does the caged bird symbolize?
data.why: The cage and clipped wings embody restriction and oppression.

data.q: Why does the caged bird sing?
opts: To express hope and demand freedom
data.why: Its song reaches beyond the cage as an act of resistance and hope.

data.q: What do “clipped wings” and “tied feet” emphasize?
data.why: The bodily restraints show that oppression is imposed.

data.q: Which structure strengthens the poem?
opts: Contrast between free and caged birds
data.why: Alternating images make inequality impossible to miss.

data.q: What is heard on the distant hill?
opts: The caged bird’s song of freedom
data.why: Although confined, the bird’s voice travels far.

poem-by-wislawa.title: The Terrorist, He’s Watching
poem-by-wislawa.by: by Wisława Szymborska · O/L Literature Interactive Quiz

data.q: Where is the terrorist?
opts: Watching a bar from across the street
data.why: He observes the targeted place from a safe distance.

data.q: What creates the poem’s suspense?
opts: A countdown to the bomb explosion
data.why: Time moves steadily toward the expected blast.

data.q: Why are people entering and leaving described?
opts: They are actors in a film
Their ordinary actions may decide who lives
data.why: Chance movements become matters of life and death.

data.q: What is disturbing about the terrorist’s viewpoint?
opts: People are treated like pieces in his plan
data.why: His detached observation reduces human lives to a calculation.

data.q: Which contrast is most important?
data.why: Normal street activity continues beside an unseen threat.

data.q: What larger idea does the poem explore?
opts: Chance, time and the fragility of life
data.why: Small accidents of timing determine survival.

Breakfast-by-Jaques-Prevert.title: Breakfast
Breakfast-by-Jaques-Prevert.by: by Jacques Prévert · O/L Literature Interactive Quiz

data.q: What is unusual about the poem’s style?
opts: It is written as a formal speech
Simple actions are listed with little explanation
data.why: The plain sequence of actions makes the emotional silence powerful.

data.q: What does the man do with the coffee?
opts: Adds milk and sugar and drinks it
data.why: The careful routine is described step by step.

data.q: How do the two people communicate?
data.why: The man says nothing, making silence central to the scene.

data.q: What does the man do before leaving?
opts: Puts on his hat and raincoat
data.why: His mechanical departure continues the emotional distance.

data.q: Why is repetition effective?
opts: It creates a joyful dance rhythm
It stresses routine, silence and emotional separation
It praises the taste of coffee
data.why: Repeated simple phrases make each action feel cold and final.

data.q: What does the speaker do at the end?
data.why: The final tears reveal the pain hidden beneath the restrained narration.

Once-upon-a-Time-by-Gabriel-Okara.title: Once Upon a Time
Once-upon-a-Time-by-Gabriel-Okara.by: by Gabriel Okara · O/L Literature Interactive Quiz

data.q: To whom does the speaker talk?
data.why: The poem is framed as a parent speaking honestly to his son.

data.q: What has changed in adult society?
opts: Warm sincerity has been replaced by artificial behaviour
data.why: The speaker contrasts former genuine feeling with modern pretence.

data.q: What do people’s eyes do while their teeth smile?
data.why: The image suggests suspicion and hidden self-interest.

data.q: What are “homeface” and “officeface”?
opts: Masks adopted for different social situations
data.why: These invented compounds show a divided, artificial identity.

data.q: What does the speaker want his son to teach him?
opts: How to laugh and smile genuinely again
How to hide his feelings better
data.why: He sees the child’s innocence as a path back to authenticity.

data.q: What is a major theme?
data.why: The poem laments social hypocrisy and longs for genuine human feeling.
